CHAPTER XXI. THE FUGITIVE MOTHER

As I hastened along, a cloud came over the moon, and from the gray dark
suddenly emerged a white figure, clasping a child to her bosom, and
stooping as she ran. She was on a line parallel with my own, but did not
perceive me as she hurried along, terror and anxiety in every movement
of her driven speed.

“She is chased!” I said to myself. “Some prowler of this terrible night
is after her!”

To follow would have added to her fright: I stepped into her track to
stop her pursuer.

As I stood for a moment looking after her through the dusk, behind me
came a swift, soft-footed rush, and ere I could turn, something sprang
over my head, struck me sharply on the forehead, and knocked me down.
I was up in an instant, but all I saw of my assailant was a vanishing
whiteness. I ran after the beast, with the blood trickling from my
forehead; but had run only a few steps, when a shriek of despair tore
the quivering night. I ran the faster, though I could not but fear it
must already be too late.

In a minute or two I spied a low white shape approaching me through the
vapour-dusted moonlight. It must be another beast, I thought at first,
for it came slowly, almost crawling, with strange, floundering leaps,
as of a creature in agony! I drew aside from its path, and waited. As it
neared me, I saw it was going on three legs, carrying its left fore-paw
high from the ground. It had many dark, oval spots on a shining white
skin, and was attended by a low rushing sound, as of water falling upon
grass. As it went by me, I saw something streaming from the lifted paw.

“It is blood!” I said to myself, “some readier champion than I has
wounded the beast!” But, strange to tell, such a pity seized me at sight
of the suffering creature, that, though an axe had been in my hand I
could not have struck at it. In a broken succession of hobbling leaps
it went out of sight, its blood, as it seemed, still issuing in a small
torrent, which kept flowing back softly through the grass beside me. “If
it go on bleeding like that,” I thought, “it will soon be hurtless!”

I went on, for I might yet be useful to the woman, and hoped also to see
her deliverer.

I descried her a little way off, seated on the grass, with her child in
her lap.

“Can I do anything for you?” I asked.

At the sound of my voice she started violently, and would have risen. I
threw myself on the ground.

“You need not be frightened,” I said. “I was following the beast when
happily you found a nearer protector! It passed me now with its foot
bleeding so much that by this time it must be all but dead!”

“There is little hope of that!” she answered, trembling. “Do you not
know whose beast she is?”

Now I had certain strange suspicions, but I answered that I knew nothing
of the brute, and asked what had become of her champion.

“What champion?” she rejoined. “I have seen no one.”

“Then how came the monster to grief?”

“I pounded her foot with a stone--as hard as I could strike. Did you not
hear her cry?”

“Well, you are a brave woman!” I answered. “I thought it was you gave
the cry!”

“It was the leopardess.”

“I never heard such a sound from the throat of an animal! it was like
the scream of a woman in torture!”

“My voice was gone; I could not have shrieked to save my baby! When I
saw the horrid mouth at my darling’s little white neck, I caught up a
stone and mashed her lame foot.”

“Tell me about the creature,” I said; “I am a stranger in these parts.”

“You will soon know about her if you are going to Bulika!” she answered.
“Now, I must never go back there!”

“Yes, I am going to Bulika,” I said, “--to see the princess.”

“Have a care; you had better not go!--But perhaps you are--! The
princess is a very good, kind woman!”

I heard a little movement. Clouds had by this time gathered so thick
over the moon that I could scarcely see my companion: I feared she was
rising to run from me.

“You are in no danger of any sort from me,” I said. “What oath would you
like me to take?”

“I know by your speech that you are not of the people of Bulika,” she
replied; “I will trust you!--I am not of them, either, else I should not
be able: they never trust any one--If only I could see you! But I like
your voice!--There, my darling is asleep! The foul beast has not hurt
her!--Yes: it was my baby she was after!” she went on, caressing the
child. “And then she would have torn her mother to pieces for carrying
her off!--Some say the princess has two white leopardesses,” she
continued: “I know only one--with spots. Everybody knows HER! If the
princess hear of a baby, she sends her immediately to suck its blood,
and then it either dies or grows up an idiot. I would have gone away
with my baby, but the princess was from home, and I thought I might wait
until I was a little stronger. But she must have taken the beast with
her, and been on her way home when I left, and come across my track. I
heard the SNIFF-SNUFF of the leopardess behind me, and ran;--oh, how I
ran!--But my darling will not die! There is no mark on her!”

“Where are you taking her?”

“Where no one ever tells!”

“Why is the princess so cruel?”

“There is an old prophecy that a child will be the death of her. That is
why she will listen to no offer of marriage, they say.”

“But what will become of her country if she kill all the babies?”

“She does not care about her country. She sends witches around to teach
the women spells that keep babies away, and give them horrible things
to eat. Some say she is in league with the Shadows to put an end to the
race. At night we hear the questing beast, and lie awake and shiver. She
can tell at once the house where a baby is coming, and lies down at the
door, watching to get in. There are words that have power to shoo her
away, only they do not always work--But here I sit talking, and the
beast may by this time have got home, and her mistress be sending the
other after us!”

As thus she ended, she rose in haste.

“I do not think she will ever get home.--Let me carry the baby for you!”
 I said, as I rose also.

She returned me no answer, and when I would have taken it, only clasped
it the closer.

“I cannot think,” I said, walking by her side, “how the brute could be
bleeding so much!”

“Take my advice, and don’t go near the palace,” she answered. “There are
sounds in it at night as if the dead were trying to shriek, but could
not open their mouths!”

She bade me an abrupt farewell. Plainly she did not want more of my
company; so I stood still, and heard her footsteps die away on the
grass.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.
[Reference Rewrite]: I mapped the architecture of the isolated villa with the hyper-focused clarity that usually precedes hypothermic shock. An instant before, the torrential Victorian night had been a blur of freezing misery; now, my senses sharpened into jagged relief. The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

"Cloud cover. Moon obscured."

A white silhouette cut through the gloom ahead, moving with frantic, jerky efficiency. A child clutched to her breast, the mother's posture bent under the weight of pure adrenaline. We shared the same vector, yet she remained blind to my presence, driven by a terror that radiated heat waves off her skin.

"She is pursued," I noted internally. "By a predator of this sector."

Pursuit protocols dictate engagement, but interference risks escalating the threat profile. Instead, I shifted laterally to intercept the trajectory of the pursuer. I paused, scanning the periphery, when a soft, fluid impact registered on my left temple. A kinetic strike. I hit the ground hard, the world tilting.

I recovered instantly, adrenaline overriding pain. All I caught was a flash of white retreating into the mist. I sprinted toward the source, blood dripping from my brow, but the chase had already peaked. A shriek tore through the night—a frequency that bypassed the auditory cortex and vibrated directly in the bone.

I accelerated, pushing past the point of rational caution. Through the vapor-thick moonlight, a low, quadrupedal form emerged. It moved with agonizing irregularity, a gait of desperate, floundering hops. Three points of contact with the earth. The fourth limb was elevated, dragging slightly.

I halted, allowing the subject to pass. Its coat was pristine white, marred by distinct, dark oval markings. A rhythmic, liquid sound accompanied its movement—the acoustic signature of rapid fluid loss. As it cleared my position, a stream of crimson trailed from the raised forelimb.

"It is hemorrhaging," I assessed clinically. "Another unit engaged the target."

Yet, a variable disrupted the tactical assessment: a surge of empathy. The biological imperative to eliminate threats clashed with the observation of acute distress. Even with a weaponized tool in hand, the decision matrix failed to execute a lethal command. The creature limped away, the flow of blood pooling softly in the grass, creating a localized hazard zone.

"If the exsanguination continues," I reasoned, "the threat vector becomes nullified within minutes."

I resumed movement. The primary objective remained the extraction of the fugitive. I located her shortly thereafter, seated on the terrain, the child secured in her lap.

"Status report?" I called out.

Her reaction was instantaneous—a violent startle response, muscles coiling to flee. I dropped to the ground, presenting a non-threatening profile.

"Stand down. No hostile intent detected. I intercepted the predator; it passed me moments ago, critically compromised by trauma to the anterior limb. Vital signs indicate imminent cessation of function."

"There is little probability of recovery," she whispered, her voice trembling. "Are you unaware of the entity's designation?"

"Suspicions exist regarding local fauna classifications," I replied, maintaining eye contact. "Identify the asset."

"I observed no third party," she stated. "Explain the mechanism of injury."

"A projectile impact. High-velocity stone. Did you not register the acoustic event?"

"You possess courage," I acknowledged. "I attributed the vocalization to you."

"The leopardess," she corrected. "Never heard such a frequency from a biological organism. It mimicked human agony."

"My vocal cords were incapacitated. Survival priority dictates silence. Upon visual confirmation of the threat vector targeting the infant—"

"Describe the specimen," I interrupted. "I am unfamiliar with this region's taxonomy."

"Familiarity increases with proximity to Bulika," she warned. "Once there, knowledge becomes redundant. I must sever ties with that location permanently."

"Destination confirmed: Bulika. Objective: Audience with the Princess."

"Cautious approach advised. However, data suggests the Princess possesses benevolent attributes."

Movement detected. Atmospheric density increased; cloud cover thickened, reducing visibility to near zero. Risk of evasion behavior escalated.

"No hostile vectors originate from me," I assured her. "Oath parameters available."

"Linguistic markers confirm non-native origin," she deduced. "Trust protocol initiated. I share similar exclusion criteria; the populace rejects external integration. Your vocal characteristics align with acceptable parameters. The infant is unconscious. The predator failed to inflict structural damage."

She cradled the child, smoothing hair from the scalp. "Intent was maternal abduction followed by filicide. Local intelligence confirms the Princess maintains a cadre of two albinos. One variant exhibits pigmentation anomalies. Universal recognition exists for this specific unit. Upon detection of an infant, deployment occurs immediately for hematological consumption. Outcome: mortality or severe cognitive regression."

"Evacuation plan aborted due to host mobility," she explained. "Princess was displaced during transit. Intercepted my trail via olfactory cues. Auditory tracking confirmed pursuit. Flight response activated."

"Prognosis for the infant remains positive. No visible trauma."

"Vector of departure unknown. Destination classified."

"Etiology of the Princess's aggression?"

"Prophecy-based risk assessment predicts offspring-induced regime collapse. Consequently, matrimonial alliances are rejected."

"Demographic sustainability threatened."

"Indifference to national continuity observed. Deployment of magical suppression agents prevents conception. Dietary restrictions enforced. Intelligence suggests collusion with Shadow entities to terminate the gene pool. Nocturnal surveillance patterns indicate predictive capability of birth events. Counter-measures involve incantatory repulsion, efficacy inconsistent."

She terminated the briefing abruptly, rising to her feet. Probability of successful return to base approaches zero.

"Offer assistance with load-bearing transfer," I proposed, initiating a stand-up maneuver.

Silence. Resistance to delegation of responsibility noted. Attempted retrieval met with increased grip tension.

"Cognitive processing error," I stated, observing the behavioral anomaly. "Hypothetical scenario: I assume custody."

No verbal response. Physical resistance intensified.

"Analysis incomplete," I muttered, resuming patrol stance. "Hemorrhage volume exceeds physiological norms for the species."

"Tactical directive: Avoidance of the Palace perimeter recommended," she instructed. "Acoustic signatures suggest necrotic activity attempting vocalization without articulation."

Farewell sequence executed. Departure confirmed. Footstep cadence indicated rapid retreat.
